sections.authorBiography: Sophocles (about 497/6 to 406/5 B.C.E.) was one of the three great tragic poets of Athens, with Aeschylus and Euripides. He was born at Colonus, just outside the city, served Athens as a general and a treasurer, and is said to have written more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. He won first prize at the City Dionysia many times and is credited with adding a third actor to the stage.

segments.script: Say: Before we start, I want to tell you about some hard parts of this play. It follows an old, blind man and his daughters at the end of a long, hard journey. It looks back on painful family events, including violence, a marriage within one family that no one knew about, and a man who hurt himself in grief, and at times characters are so full of sorrow that they say they wish they could die. segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, / What region, say, whose city have we reached” slowly and put it in my own words: A blind, aging father asks his daughter what land and what city they have reached. He does not know where he is, and he has to ask. Next, craft. I notice the opening is a question, not a command: the man who once answered the Sphinx now depends on Antigone for the simple fact of place. The strongest word is “blind”: “old blind sire” tells us his condition before we hear his name, and it explains why the daughter, not the king, must see the road. Then, effect. What do lines 1–2 reveal about the beggar at the sacred grove? My answer: The king who once solved riddles must now ask where he is. The first thing we learn is dependence and exile: the sacred grove is still only a place they have reached, and he cannot see it.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Oedipus at Colonus.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Oedipus at Colonus: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Oedipus at Colonus has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to refuge and hospitality.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Oedipus at Colonus. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to refuge and hospitality.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Oedipus at Colonus.

He asks to be kept within the paths of right, where counsel may be freely exchanged, and not to have to fight with fate and fortune. “Safe within the paths of right; / Counsel freely may exchange / Nor with fate and fortune fight.” (lines 180–182). The wording treats lawful speech as a shelter: if they will hear him in the right path, he will not have to contend with fortune as an enemy in that moment. The elders' next word is a halt at the rocky floor.
To remain in the chorus's charge, or to come with Theseus
Here shall he vanquish those who cast him forth

He says he would recoil from no such request, because he too was reared, like Oedipus, in exile and in foreign lands. “I too was reared, / Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands” (lines 583–584). The comparison is the ground of welcome: not pity alone, and not a legal trick, but a remembered exile that lets him recognise the man before him. The grant of protection follows from that recognition in this episode.

He makes the promised worth depend on the gods still being true: if Zeus is Zeus and Phoebus still speaks true. “If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true.” (line 644). A few lines later he adds that this will hold except the gods themselves shall play him false. “Except the gods themselves shall play me false.” (line 650). The gift he offers Athens is therefore a religious confidence, not a private boast he can enforce alone, and not a later report already accomplished.
Disdain to visit this heaven-favoured plain

The tree grows unpruned and untamed, and it is self-nurtured year by year, so the ode presents it as living from this soil itself, not as an imported or forced plant. “Self-nurtured year by year;” (line 724). Together with the claim that it is unnamed in Asian soil and unclaimed by Pelops' isle, the wording makes the olive a native, enduring growth of the fatherland, not a decoration added for this scene alone.

After saying that neither youth nor withering age destroys the tree, the chorus adds that the Grey-eyed Goddess herself defends it. “And the Grey-eyed Goddess herself defends.” (line 728). The plant is not only hardy; it is under Athena's own care. The defence is religious and civic in the song, not a later battle already shown, and it belongs to the ode's praise of a land that can keep what it has grown.

The close boasts of gifts prized by the fatherland: the iron bit for the mouth of horses, and the oar-blade, as they dance along the brine. “For the mouth of horses the iron bit;” (line 735). The land is praised not only for flowers and a sacred tree, but for horsemanship and seafaring. The boast is a song of what this soil teaches and defends, offered to a worn stranger as the character of the place that has received him, not as a later campaign already fought.
He calls it a front of brass, whose subtle tongue would twist every plea
Their sovereign may need to intervene

He says that with a just quarrel, weakness conquers might. “With a just quarrel weakness conquers might.” (line 920). The line is a self-justifying proverb: he presents force as weakness in a just cause, even as he has already seized a daughter and is trying to take the other. The scene lets us hear the claim and see the act together, so the proverb can be judged against the violence it excuses.

Theseus tells him that, having come unto a state that champions right, he should have asked, for every action, a warranty of law. “Unto a State that champions right and asks / For every action warranty of law,” (lines 957–958). The standard is civic: force in Athens must answer to law, even when a foreign kinsman claims a just quarrel. The rebuke belongs to this episode and does not yet narrate a later war at Thebes.
Pallas

They say that today, today, Zeus worketh some great thing, and that this day shall victory bring. “Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing / This day shall victory bring.” (lines 1132–1133). The hope is present and divine: the day's work is imagined as Zeus's, and as a victory still being asked for, until the escort is seen. It is not a later campaign already fought in another land.

They picture Theseus's chieftain's men, with each bridle flashing and each gallant knight charging. “Theseus our chieftain’s men.” (line 1118). “Flashes each bridle bright,” (line 1119). The image is bright and swift, a civic force in motion, offered as a hope the song can almost see. It remains a choral vision until the last line announces the escort.

It opens by imagining the flying foe and the battle roar, and it prays the gods to cherish rites and to help the chase; it closes when an escort with the maids draws near. “O when the flying foe,” (line 1092). “For lo, an escort with the maids draws near.” (line 1152). The movement is from alarm to arrival. The song does not linger on the violence as a spectacle; it asks for a rescue and then sees the daughters brought back.
All matters, great or small

Theseus asks why he is so loth to hear the man; Oedipus answers that the voice grates on a father's ears, that he has come to loathe it, and that he should not be forced to yield. “That voice, O king, grates on a father’s ears; / I have come to loathe it. Force me not to yield.” (lines 1236–1237). The reluctance is personal and already sure of the speaker, before the son is officially received; it prepares the later hearing without yet speaking the curse.

He says the man has found asylum, and he warns Oedipus not to fail in due reverence to the god. “But he hath found asylum. O beware, / And fail not in due reverence to the god.” (lines 1238–1239). The warning makes the hearing a religious duty as well as a favour: the suppliant is under a god's protection, so refusal is not only a family matter. The line belongs to this episode's pressure to admit the son, not to a later curse already spoken.

She asks her father to yield, because just suitors should not need to be importunate, and because the one who takes a favour should not lack the grace to make return. “O yield to us; just suitors should not need / To be importunate, nor he that takes / A favour lack the grace to make return.” (lines 1260–1262). The argument binds the hearing to courtesy and to return of grace, after she has already asked him to heed her though she is young. It wins a grudging consent, not a blessing on the war.
A grievous load, with scant pleasures and heavier pains

It says the long years heap up a grievous load, scant pleasures and heavier pains, till not one joy remains for him who lingers on life's weary road. “Till not one joy remains / For him who lingers on life’s weary road” (lines 1276–1277). The picture is of joy worn out by lingering. Taught in this episode's wake, it names what a long life can cost, especially for a guest the next stanza will compare to a beaten headland.

When youth passes, troubles follow on troubles, toils on toils, and pain for ever pain; then the tale of life is made of envy, sedition, strife, carnage and war. “Troubles on troubles follow, toils on toils, / Pain, pain for ever pain;” (lines 1289–1290). “Envy, sedition, strife, / Carnage and war, make up the tale of life.” (lines 1292–1293). The movement is from private weariness to civic violence. It is a choral vision of a human common lot, not a later battle already shown.

After the general meditation, the chorus says such ills are not theirs alone; the guest has known them too. “Such ills not I alone, / He too our guest hath known,” (lines 1298–1299). The turn makes the ode local and ethical: the dark common lot is used to recognise this one beaten life. It is pity for a known guest. The headland image that follows keeps the recognition concrete, as weather and tide.
From Argos, with seven champion captains at his side
They have tended him; without them he would have had no aid from the son

He calls him a villain, and he asks whether, when the son had the sovereignty that the brother now holds, he did not drive his own father out. “O villain, when thou hadst the sovereignty / That now thy brother holdeth in thy stead, / Didst thou not drive me, thine own father, out,” (lines 1406–1408). The charge is exile and neglect, set against the present plea. The curse that follows is prepared by this recalling of the past, not by a later battle already shown.

He meets the silence as a refusal already aimed at him. He asks why his father is silent, whether he will dismiss him in mute disdain, and he tries to move a sullen, obstinate silence. “Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away,” (line 1329). “In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath?” (line 1331). The wound is named before the long speech of the curse: not a debate yet, but no word at all.
charge

He says his life hath turned the scale, and he would do all he promised Theseus and his before he dies. “My life hath turned the scale. I would do all / I promised thee and thine before I die.” (lines 1558–1559). The wording holds a promise kept at an appointed time. The charge that follows is the performing of that promise, in this scene, as the signs have come.

He asks that they set forth to the spot without longer delay, because the god within him goads him. “But to the spot—the god within me goads— / Let us set forth nor longer hesitate.” (lines 1590–1591). “Goads” makes the movement an inner divine urging, not a human itinerary he has invented, and not a recovery of ordinary eyesight. The line should be taught as a summons accepted.

Theseus says he must believe him, having found him often a true prophet, and then he asks what must be done. “I must believe thee, having found thee oft / A prophet true; then speak what must be done.” (lines 1566–1567). Trust follows a record of truthfulness, and it opens the way for the charge and the promise Oedipus still means to perform. The scene presents belief and duty together; it does not yet report a later passing as accomplished.
legends

After picturing the hound that glares at all comers, the elders ask a precise mercy: let this one man go unharmed to the fields below. “At all comers, let him go / Scathless to the fields below.” (lines 1620–1621). “Scathless” means without hurt; the request is that the gateway not wound him. That is a petition addressed to a guardian.

They address a fell watch-dog of the gates of hell, and they picture it gnarling in its cavernous lair. “Queen infernal, and thou fell / Watch-dog of the gates of hell,” (lines 1616–1617). “Gnarling in thy cavernous lair” (line 1619). The image is fierce, but the petition that follows is not a wish to see anyone destroyed. The hound remains a guardian in the song; the prayer asks it not to treat this stranger as prey.

It is a religious song of escort, spoken in the city's voice. It starts in uncertainty “If mortal prayers are heard in hell,” (line 1606) and closes by addressing a “Giver of eternal sleep” (line 1625), after asking that a going already signalled be received without further harm. Those are petitions about how the underworld might receive him.
brazen

The messenger says Theseus repressed his tears and swore to be their constant friend. “His tears and swore to be their constant friend.” (line 1681). The oath is a pledge of care for the living, given at the edge of the end, and it is not a request that anyone share the passing. Later he will keep another charge about the hidden place; this line records the friendship sworn beforehand.

After mourning has an end and no wail rose, there is a moment of silence; then a voice summons him, and with sudden dread the hair of all stands up. The call comes now loud, now low, and oft, naming him twice and asking why they tarry, for the passing has been delayed too long. “A moment there was silence; suddenly / A voice that summoned him;” (lines 1667–1668). “Oedipus, Oedipus, why tarry we? / Too long, too long thy passing is delayed.” (lines 1671–1672). The voice is not a human command; the messenger treats it as the summons of the god.

He tells the daughters that Oedipus charged him straitly that no mortal should approach the sacred portal or greet the hidden tomb with funeral litanies; he then says the God of Oaths heard that promise, and he pledged his word to Zeus. “Charged me straitly that no mortal / Should approach the sacred portal,” (lines 1812–1813). “The God of Oaths this promise heard, / And to Zeus I pledged my word.” (lines 1818–1819). The secrecy is a kept oath, tied to the city's rest, not a wish to abandon the daughters.

A fair defence can call it both. Theseus tells them to go in peace, and he will spare no toil and zealous care, but will attend to all their needs, gladdening in the grave his friend. The chorus then bids them wail no more, and says that all is ordered for the best. “Go in peace; nor will I spare / Aught of toil and zealous care,” (lines 1826–1827). “Wail no more, let sorrow rest, / All is ordered for the best.” (lines 1830–1831). Consolation here is not cheerfulness. The close holds care and an ordered peace together with the loss still in view.

After warning that he would see the visitor out of harm, the stranger reads past the ruined appearance to a judgment of nobility, and he tells him to tarry while the nearby burghers are sought. “For by thy looks, marred though they be by fate, / I judge thee noble: tarry where thou art,” (lines 76–77). The contrast is the point: fate has marred the looks, but the stranger still finds a nobility there, and that reading is what lets him leave the man seated until the locals decide.

He asks her to stay him and set him down if she sees a resting place on common ground or by some sacred grove, and then to discover where they have come, because strangers must inquire of denizens and do as they are bid. “Stay me and set me down. Need and courtesy are held together: he wants rest, but he also states a rule of inquiry and obedience for an outsider. The later clash over the holy seat tests that rule; it is not yet a later king's grant.

Speak, for he stands on the slippery verge

Pressed to say of what stock he comes, he begins a name and does not even finish it: “Know’st one of Laius’—” (line 209). The chorus breaks in with a cry, “Ha! Who!” (line 210). The warning is that cities and friendships can change, so the gift he offers must be kept with that change in mind. It is counsel to a host, not a report of a war already fought.

The tree is said to feed the land's boys, and then the chorus adds that neither youth nor withering age destroys it. “Nor youth nor withering age destroys” (line 726). items.prompt: Analyse “Myself anon without a guiding hand / Will take thee to the spot where I must end”. What does Oedipus claim, and how should it be taught?
items.expected: He claims that he himself, soon, without a guiding hand, will take Theseus to the spot where he must end. “Myself anon without a guiding hand / Will take thee to the spot where I must end.” (lines 1570–1571). The claim is a reversal of being led, and a placing of the charge at a particular spot in this land. It should be taught as a god-sent path he can walk, not as a recovery of ordinary sight.

items.prompt: Theseus reports a promise that the realm shall be at rest if he keeps a charge, and he has pledged that word to Zeus. Does the close present that kept silence as a civic gift? Argue from this scene, without turning the hidden tomb into a puzzle to solve on stage.
items.expected: Yes, in the form this play allows. Theseus reports that if he keeps the hest he shall hold his realm at rest; he then says the God of Oaths heard the promise, and he pledged his word to Zeus. “If thou keep’st my hest / Thou shalt hold thy realm at rest.” (lines 1816–1817). “The God of Oaths this promise heard, / And to Zeus I pledged my word.” (lines 1818–1819). The protection is not a visible monument. It is a silence kept by the king, offered as a defence of the land, after a painless passing that only he has seen. The gift is the oath, not a grave the audience is invited to find.

answerKey.answer: Suffering, and last not least, true nobility

She hushes him, because she sees grey-beards on their way, their errand to spy out the resting-place. “Hush! for I see some grey-beards on their way, / Their errand to spy out our resting-place.” (lines 109–110). He says he will be mute, and that she shall guide his steps off the public road, until he has learned their drift. “I will be mute, and thou shalt guide my steps / Into the covert from the public road,” (lines 111–112). The scene ends in caution and listening, not in a public claim already accepted.

In the prayer, after calling on the gentle daughters of primeval Night, he turns to Athens by name, as namesake of great Pallas and first of cities, and he asks pity for a dishonoured shade. “Hear, namesake of great Pallas; Athens, first / Of cities, pity this dishonoured shade, / The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.” (lines 106–108). The petition is civic as well as religious: the city itself is asked to pity a shade, not to restore a throne, and the wording holds honour and dishonour in one address.

In the prayer, once the stranger has gone, he says Phoebus, when he told the miseries to come, also spoke of this respite after many years: some haven in a far-off land, a rest vouchsafed at last by dread divinities. “Spake of this respite after many years, / Some haven in a far-off land, a rest / Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities.” (lines 88–90). The lines should be taught as a promised rest at the end of wandering. In this scene the haven is still a hope named in prayer, not a later report of the end.

Both are present and should be held together. At the opening he still has to ask what region and whose city they have reached, and he tells Antigone that strangers must inquire. “What region, say, whose city have we reached?” (line 2). After the stranger has named the goddesses and gone, he prays that he now recognises as theirs the sign that led his wanderings to this grove. “And now I recognise as yours the sign / That led my wanderings to this your grove;” (lines 96–97). Inquiry comes first; recognition is claimed only after the place has been named. The scene does not yet show a later king's welcome, or the end itself.

The chorus has asked of what stock he comes, what man's son; that is the question he has been reluctant to meet. “Say of what stock thou comest, what man’s son—” (line 204). His answer is a cry to Antigone that now they are undone. “Ah me, my daughter, now we are undone!” (line 205). He already knows that the name, once spoken, will undo the fragile safety of being only a nameless trespasser; the line is a recognition of that cost, just before he agrees to speak.

The halt freezes him at a marked line: no further than that rocky floor. “Halt! Go no further than that rocky floor.” (line 183). He asks whether he should stay where he now is, and they tell him to advance no more; he then asks if he may sit, and they direct him sideways to the ledge. The questioning of name and lineage happens only after he has been placed, crouching, at that edge. The staging turns a hunt-like entrance into a controlled examination at a boundary.

They require him to honour whatever the State honours, and to hate all that she frowns on. “Honour whatso’er the State / Honours, all she frowns on hate.” (lines 177–178). The demand is civic and present: the stranger must take the city's likings and dislikings as his measure, not import another rule, and not treat the grove as ground he may define for himself. It is spoken before they know his name, so the claim is general; later, once the name is known, that same civic voice will add fear to law.

It is a discovery that turns into an expulsion. The elders begin by hunting an unseen trespasser and questioning him; once the lineage is out, they order father and daughter out of the land. “Forth from our borders speed ye both!” (line 220). The same civic voice that had been setting limits and asking for a name now uses that name as a reason to drive them away. A fair reading can also note the limit: pity is later admitted, but the command to depart has already been spoken, and they will not unsay it in this scene.
Hale him hence, against Theseus's will

He says that even if the foemen's words are brave, boasting to bring Oedipus back, they are like to find the seas between them wide and hard to sail. “Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find / The seas between us wide and hard to sail.” (lines 690–691). He adds that his name, though he be distant, warrants the guest from harm. “Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.” (line 694). The protection is a king's purpose in this land, not a later battle already shown, and not a dismissal from the grove.

He asks them to see his deeds as those of a man more sinned against than sinning. “Deeds of a man more sinned against than sinning” (line 258). The wording does not deny that acts were done; it asks for a weighing of what was done to him against what he did, and it belongs with his claim of self-defence and of acting without knowledge. The line should be taught as this episode's defence of intent, not as a verdict imported from a later play.

Theseus grants the full rights of citizen and will not spurn the favours offered; Oedipus, received, says that here he shall vanquish those who cast him forth. “But grant him the full rights of citizen;” (line 661). “Here shall I vanquish those who cast me forth.” (line 670). The vanquishing is tied to being held in this land, under a god's word, not to Oedipus taking up arms on stage. The two speeches together recast the outcast as a guest whose worth will tell against Thebes, without showing that later conflict as already accomplished in this scene.

The first gift named is rest, offered to a stranger worn with toil, and only then is the land called goodliest. “Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil,” (lines 695–696). The order matters: the song meets weariness first, and praise of Colonus follows as the ground of that rest. It is a welcome, not a hunt, and it does not yet tell what a later messenger will say of an end.

The tree grows unpruned and untamed, and the next line calls it a terror to foemen's spear. “Terror to foemen’s spear,” (line 721). The olive is not only a peaceful emblem; the ode makes it a living defence that should frighten an enemy. The boast is civic and almost martial, yet still a plant's boast, not a report of a battle already won on stage. It prepares the later claim that Athena herself defends the tree.

The ode insists the tree is unnamed in Asian soil and unclaimed by Pelops' Dorian isle, yet self-nurtured year by year here. The contrast locates the olive as uniquely Attic: not a borrowed eastern wonder, and not a Peloponnesian prize, but a growth of this fatherland. The patriotism is made by exclusion as well as by praise, and it should be taught as the song's way of saying whose tree this is, not as a later campaign already fought.

Yes, at least in the civic voice of this song. Elders who had hunted a trespasser now praise the same land as a rest for a worn stranger, a heaven-favoured plain, and a fatherland whose tree feeds its boys and is itself defended. The fear of the holy ground is not erased, but it is joined to pride and welcome. A careful reading can also note the limit: a short ode is not the whole play, and it does not yet show whether that welcome will hold when force arrives.
They will not let her, father

He reminds Creon that in old days, when he was distraught by self-wrought woes, he yearned for exile as a glad release, and the favour he then craved was refused. “In old days when by self-wrought woes distraught, / I yearned for exile as a glad release,” (lines 783–784). The present invitation to come home is judged by that past refusal: the offer is late, and it is suspect because it arrives when Thebes wants him, not when he asked to go. The argument is about timing and motive in this episode, not about a later grave already assigned.

He accuses him of a brazen face and a subtle tongue that would twist every plea of right to his own advantage. “O front of brass, thy subtle tongue would twist / To thy advantage every plea of right” (lines 779–780). The charge is rhetorical: right is not denied as a word, but is said to be twisted. That accusation frames all of Creon's later claims of warrant and just quarrel, so the class can hear those claims as the twisting the opening insult named.

The test is the point of the scene. Creon seizes a daughter and claims a warrant for the wrong; Theseus answers that a state which champions right asks, for every action, a warranty of law. “Unto a State that champions right and asks / For every action warranty of law,” (lines 957–958). Athens is asked to make its titles good, not by a speech alone, but by refusing to let force go scathless. The episode shows that test under way; it does not yet narrate later campaigns beyond this land.

After steeds, gods, and a promised victory, the last line is almost plain: an escort with the maids draws near. “For lo, an escort with the maids draws near.” (line 1152). The effect is to answer the prayer in the form the play can show—the daughters coming back—without staging the fight itself. The close is relief and arrival, not a boast that every enemy has already been destroyed offstage.

Zeus is asked as the power who worketh some great thing today and whose day shall bring victory; Apollo is asked as hunter. “Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing” (line 1132). “Hear, Apollo, hunter, hear,” (line 1144). One address is about a day's great work; the other fits the chase. The song holds a civic hope under two names, and it should be taught as prayer, not as a report that the gods have already finished the work before the escort appears.

Early in the song the chorus bids the powers cherish the mystic rites, even as it imagines a chase after a robber band. The rescue is therefore asked for inside a religious frame: the land's rites, not only its pride, are what the violence has offended. The prayer wants the daughters back, and it wants the holy order of the place upheld. That double asking is the ode's way of making the seizure more than a family quarrel, without yet telling a later passing or a later tomb.

It completes that test in the form a choral song can complete it: the city, having been asked to make its titles good, is now seen bringing the maids back under escort. Earlier the song had hoped to behold a rescue of the captives twain. “Rescue by might and main / Maidens, the captives twain.” (lines 1110–1111). “I shall behold the twain” (line 1129). The closing arrival fulfills that hope on stage, without staging the fight itself. A careful reading should also note the limit: the next episode will still have to deal with a suppliant son. The ode answers the seizure; it does not end the play.
The words have told him who the suppliant is

She asks him to heed her though she is young in years, to let the prince have his will, and to pay what in Theseus's eyes is service to the god; and she asks, for their sake also, that their brother may come. “O heed me, father, though I am young in years.” (line 1240). “For our sake also let our brother come.” (line 1243). Youth, civic duty, piety, and family are stacked in one appeal, which is why the hearing, when it is granted, is granted to more than one claimant.

She has just told him to think on the woe his sire and mother brought him, and she says he will draw this lesson without fail: of evil passion evil is the end. “Of evil passion evil is the end.” (line 1257). The maxim is aimed at his present loathing as much as at a past history: she wants him to see that a savage mood, if not yielded, ends in evil. The line is persuasion, not a curse already spoken, and it should be taught as her attempt to avert a new harshness by recalling an old one.

Theseus first warns that the suppliant has found asylum and that due reverence to the god must not fail; at the close he promises that Oedipus's life is safe while any god saves his own. “But he hath found asylum. O beware, / And fail not in due reverence to the god.” (lines 1238–1239). “Thy life is safe while any god saves mine.” (line 1269). The son cannot be refused as if he were only a hated voice, and the father cannot be handed over as if he were only a prize. The episode holds both protections at once, and it leaves the hearing itself still to come.

After the headland and the whelming tide, the song says he is overborne by every wind of heaven, some from the sunset, some from orient morn, some from the noonday glow, some from Rhipean gloom of everlasting snow. “Some from the sunset, some from orient morn, / Some from the noonday glow.” (lines 1305–1306). The four quarters make the buffeting complete: no side is spared. The close is an image of exposure, not a map of a later tomb.

The ode has already named pain, envy, war; then it says last comes the worst and most abhorred stage of unregarded age, joyless, companionless and slow, of woes the crowning woe. “Last comes the worst and most abhorred stage / Of unregarded age,” (lines 1294–1295). What makes it worst, in the song, is not a hidden crime but being unregarded, without joy or companion, and slow. The diction is social as well as bodily. It should be taught as a lament over neglect, especially once the next lines turn toward a known guest.

It should be read as a choral statement of a common bound. The line comes after the claim that one doom awaits all, for marriage bell and funeral knell; it names death as a deliverer who frees all at last. “Death the deliverer freeth all at last.” (line 1283). In a tragedy, that can be a grim consolation about a shared fate. The class should hear the darkness of the line and keep it in the song that is about to name the guest.

It means the general vision is already ethical and dramatic, not a detachable essay. A father has just been persuaded, grudgingly, to hear a son he loathes; the chorus then sings of a weary road, of public strife, and of a guest buffeted like a headland. “He too our guest hath known,” (line 1299). The song places that coming hearing inside a view of a life already overloaded. It does not speak the curse, and it does not tell a later passing; it asks us to see the man who must still receive a suppliant as one who has already been lashed by every wind.
It is so, and stay him not; the road he chooses, he will take

He presents himself as a figure of want: he bears a wallet against hunger's pinch. “He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch.” (line 1320). The detail is meant to stir pity and to rhyme with his father's beggar's state, before he names the seven captains and the war. The later curse will judge that resemblance as a tactic; in these opening lines it is still his chosen image of himself.

He does not only ask for a word; he names the silence as mute disdain, and as a dismissal already under way. “In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath?” (line 1331). The phrase turns absence of speech into a judged insult, so that the son can feel refused before the father has begun the curse. It is a rhetorical move as well as a wound, and it sets the temperature of the scene before the long speeches start.

A fair defence can call it both. Oedipus charges the son with driving him out when he had the sovereignty, and he then invokes a curse already launched to fight for him now. “Didst thou not drive me, thine own father, out,” (line 1408). “Such curse I now invoke to fight for me,” (line 1429). The justice he claims is real in his account of neglect; the form it takes is a doom sent onward into a war not yet fought. The scene should be taught as a spoken future, not as a report that the two have already fallen.

She asks what solemn charge he would impress on the prince. “What solemn charge would’st thou impress on him?” (line 1540). The question pulls the promised trust into the open before the king is fully employed on stage, so that the audience hears the need for a charge, not only the need for a hurried coming. It organises the scene without inventing the summons, and it does not yet tell how a later report will describe the end.

He claims that he himself, soon, without a guiding hand, will take Theseus to the spot where he must end. “Myself anon without a guiding hand / Will take thee to the spot where I must end.” (lines 1570–1571). finalPaper.exemplar: The king who once solved riddles must now ask where he is. The forbidden grove of the Furies becomes his place of rest. The text makes this visible when it says “Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, / What region, say, whose city have we reached” (Prologue, lines 1–2). Blind and old, Oedipus arrives with Antigone at a grove near Athens. A local man tells him it is holy ground of the Eumenides and that he must leave. Oedipus refuses: Apollo foretold that he would end his days here, a blessing to his hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
